Issued at 333 AM CST Wed Nov 11 2026

A pronounced shortwave trough will dive southeastward into 
Illinois and Indiana today, bringing along a deepening surface 
low that will track across central portions of both states. A 
wedge of dry low-level air will keep the initial radar echoes 
that encroach upon our forecast area as virga or sprinkles, but 
within a few hours, sufficient top-down saturation will occur 
for a period of wetting rain showers to cross our CWA from west 
to east between the late morning and early evening. A pocket of 
slightly steepened mid-level lapse rates tied to the incoming 
vort max could result in a few lightning strikes occurring in 
our southernmost counties this afternoon near the surface low. 
If the surface low manages to take a track that is a little 
farther to the north than the consensus of the latest hi-res 
model guidance and the associated warm front creeps into our 
far southern CWA, then an isolated strong to severe storm could 
not be ruled out near and south of the US-24 corridor this 
afternoon. However, the much more likely outcome at this time 
is that the modest warm sector surface-based instability and 
associated marginal severe thunderstorm threat will remain to 
the south of our area, near and south of the I-74 corridor.

Later today, a lobe of a sprawling upper-level trough over 
eastern Canada will veer southward into the Upper Midwest and 
Great Lakes, bringing a shot of colder air into the region. 
While the magnitude of the colder temperatures associated with 
this inbound air mass will not be of the same caliber as the air
mass that resulted in a notable lake effect snow event around 
this time last year, it will still nevertheless be cold enough 
to get the lake effect machine going and cause some areas to see
their first snowflakes of this cool season. Before the main 
lake effect band becomes established though, a wave or two of 
lake-enhanced showers (possibly coupled with non-lake-influenced
convective showers) will likely affect areas well inland from 
Lake Michigan on Thursday as an inverted trough axis comes 
crashing into the area. Rain should be the predominant 
precipitation type observed with this, but depending on how 
quickly this initial activity arrives, could not rule out a few 
snowflakes being observed in some locations Thursday morning. 
Blustery northerly winds are also expected throughout the day on
Thursday and will prevent temperatures from climbing much (if 
at all) during the daytime.

In the meantime, the mean longwave eastern Canadian trough will
be in the process of sagging southward and re-centering itself 
over the eastern Great Lakes. As this occurs, a secondary 
embedded shortwave will plunge southward from western Ontario, 
sending a reinforcing shot of colder air into the western Great 
Lakes that will only enhance the already favorable lake effect 
thermodynamic parameter space over Lake Michigan. The prolonged 
northerly fetch over the lake will favor a robust, dominant 
single lake effect band that should largely focus into northwest
Indiana from Thursday evening all the way through Friday 
night/early Saturday, though occasional westward wobbles in the 
primarily lake convergence axis could still steer the associated
precipitation towards and potentially across the Illinois- 
Indiana state line at times. It should also be noted that the 
deep lake-induced convective cloud depths and water surface-850
mb temperature differentials pushing 20C could also support a 
potential for waterspouts over Lake Michigan during this lake 
effect precipitation event.

Air temperatures will cool into the 20s and 30s Thursday night 
as cold air advection continues off of north-northwesterly 
winds. This will trend the lake effect band towards a 
heterogeneous composition of precipitation types, with some 
locations (especially those farther away from the lakeshore) 
possibly seeing a changeover to outright snow at some point 
Thursday night. However, with lake temperatures in the low-mid 
50s in the lead up to this event, thermal profiles downwind of 
the lake look like they will remain marginal at best for wet 
snow accumulations to occur throughout this lake effect event. 
Antecedent ground temperatures will be fairly mild as well, 
which will make it all the more difficult for slushy 
accumulations to be realized on paved surfaces, including 
roadways. That said, given the fairly robust lake effect 
thermodynamics at play, hefty precipitation rates may be 
observed at times, and that could prove to be just enough for 
the less-than-favorable air and ground temperatures to be 
overcome in some locations in the event that temperatures 
Thursday night (and again Friday night) end up verifying 
towards the lower end of the spectrum of the latest forecast 
guidance. Ultimately, while an impactful wet lake effect snow
